Source presence or link acceptance alone is insufficient.

status_policy: All topics below remain incomplete. partially_supported means a reviewed official source is relevant but issue-level adequacy is not established. unresolved means no adequate source-backed evidence has yet been identified for that layer. topics.label: Directive scope, EU/EEA/Swiss scope, family categories, and return situations

primary_law.note: Act Articles 1–3 define the EU, EEA and Swiss scope and expressly address family members of a Bulgarian citizen after free movement; Additional Provisions § 1(1) defines spouses/cohabiting partners, descendants and dependent ascendants. Article 5 separately covers dependent/household members and serious-health carers, requires detailed individual review and reasoned denial. Crosswalked to Directive Articles 2–3. The legal classification of the Act’s documented “factual cohabitation” routes and the precise return-situation scope of Article 1 remain open.

implementing_rule.note: Instruction №8121з-1276 Articles 3–5 distinguishes family members who have or have not exercised free movement and expressly labels Article 3(2) persons “beneficiaries”; it supplies document routes but does not resolve the legal classification of all cohabitation/partnership evidence, the precise return situation, or each current operational requirement. Its accepted consolidation ends at SG 29/2021.

procedure.note: Act Article 5(2) requires detailed examination of personal circumstances for extended-family and cohabitation applicants; a refusal must be reasoned and is subject to judicial legality review under the APC. The MVR service and Instruction provide application routes, but current category-specific evidence/checklists and return-situation handling are not fully documented.

remedy_or_practice.note: VAS Decision №11351/2019 is one final Bulgarian example applying the spouse concept to derivative residence for a same-sex spouse, under the pre-SG 34/2019 Act version and for residence purposes only; it is not a broad family-status survey or a general return-situation ruling. CJEU Coman, O. and B., and Singh provide relevant EU-law context; Bulgarian practice on mobile Bulgarian returnees and Article 3(2) cases remains unreviewed.

open_issues: Map the Act’s core family definition and Article 5 facilitation route to Directive Articles 2–3, including whether documented factual cohabitation is treated as a registered partner, a durable partner, or another national route; assess the relevant evidence and reasoned individual examination without conflating facilitated residence with an automatic right.

Resolve the scope of Act Article 1 for family members of a mobile Bulgarian national, including its exact wording and applicant-nationality limits, against Article 21 TFEU and O. and B. (C-456/12), Singh (C-370/90), and Coman (C-673/16). The existing VAS decision is limited to the pre-2019 version and does not close this issue.

Confirm the treaty instruments and exact family-member scope for EEA/Swiss citizens, then search official Bulgarian decisions and procedures for return cases, extended-family/household applicants, and durable relationships.

topics.label: Entry, exit, visa exemption, and facilitation for qualifying family members

primary_law.note: The accepted Bulgarian Visa Ordinance is cross-referenced to Directive 2004/38/EC Articles 5(2) and 10 and the Visa Code. Council Decision (EU) 2024/210 made the listed Visa Code acquis applicable to Bulgaria on 31 March 2024; the Bulgaria non-applicability sentence in Commission Notice C/2023/1392 is now outdated. The full article-level concordance, applicant-class scope, and Bulgarian implementation of Regulation 2023/2667 remain open.

implementing_rule.note: Ordinance Articles 20(2)(4) and 23(3) provide a specified insurance-proof exemption and direct access without prior appointment for qualifying family/household members. MFA guidance adds means/accommodation/transport, insurance and family fee exemptions; exact applicant scope and interaction with Visa Code/Directive fee and provider-charge rules remain open.

procedure.note: Current central MFA guidance was rechecked 25 October 2026. It states general 15-day submission and possible appointment instructions, limited family evidence, and the prior-consultation list. It does not explain the qualifying family-member accelerated route or how the general timing/appointment text is scoped; mission-specific instructions, representation and prior-consultation handling remain open.

remedy_or_practice.note: The current MFA page identifies appeal routes to the MFA or Administrative Court Sofia-city. Directive Article 5(2) and the 2024 Visa Code Handbook inform accelerated handling, but national deadlines, competent forum, costs, and reviewed decisions remain open.

open_issues: Complete the applicant-class and provision crosswalk for Directive 2004/38 Articles 5(2) and 10, Visa Code Articles 9, 16, 17 and 32, the Visa Code Handbook I, and Bulgarian Ordinance Articles 20(2)(4) and 23(3); preserve the 31 March 2024 Schengen start date and the limited Article 3 exception in Decision 2024/210.

Verify the scope of the MFA’s relationship-only evidence, means/accommodation/transport and insurance exemptions, family visa-fee waiver, and prior-consultation rules against national text and EU law; separate visa-fee waiver from optional external-provider service charges.
Review border-entry evidence, mission representation, online-application implementation and remedies for qualifying family members; do not infer operational coverage from central web guidance.

topics.label: Residence conditions, worker/self-employed/student/economically inactive categories, and proof

primary_law.note: The accepted Act Articles 7–8 provide continued residence up to five years and the worker/self-employed, sufficient-resources plus insurance, student, and retained-worker categories; Article 8(2) separately addresses accompanying/joining family members. Article 5 provides a detailed review route for other dependent/household or serious-health relatives and durable partners. Crosswalked to Directive Articles 7–8, 14 and 25 in source-dependencies.json. Legal review remains open on proof limits, individualized resource assessment, student status, retained-worker wording, and the qualifying conditions for non-EU family members.

implementing_rule.note: Instruction №8121з-1276, Article 6 lists employer/self-employment evidence, health cover and resources for inactive applicants, and enrolment/insurance/resources for students; Articles 6a–7 address non-EU family-member applications. The Instruction’s evidence lists are compared with Directive Article 8’s limited-document rules, Article 8(4)’s individualized resource assessment, and Article 10; the 2021 cutoff and exact current administrative demands remain open.

procedure.note: Act Article 9 requires application within three months of entry, provides same-day issuance, a seven-day cure for incomplete documents, reasoned refusal and an Administrative Procedure Code challenge; follow-up checks require data supporting a reasoned inference of a residence-rule breach. The Instruction sets a three-month filing route and itemized evidence, including a fee only where information cannot be checked administratively. Current forms, resource-assessment practice, fee application, and evidence demands beyond the Directive Article 8 list are not verified.

remedy_or_practice.note: The Act provides a reasoned refusal and APC challenge after the seven-day cure period. One final VAS decision on derivative residence under a historical version is not evidence about worker, self-employed, student or sufficient-resources decisions. No screened Bulgarian decision addressing Article 7 eligibility tests or additional evidence demands is recorded.

open_issues: Compare Act Articles 5 and 7–8 with Directive Articles 3(2), 7 and 14: determine when the principal EU citizen must meet an Article 7 category for a non-EU family member, how student-family limits apply, and distinguish facilitated residence for extended family/durable partners from an automatic residence entitlement.

Map the exact permissible documents and individualized assessment for resources and insurance. Check Directive Article 8(3)–(4) against the national Act and Instruction, including whether any fixed amount or unnecessary evidence is requested in practice; verify retained-worker conditions and recognized educational establishments.

Verify current application forms, appointment and filing channels, fees, cure process and appeal route from current official material, then screen repeatable official-court searches for residence eligibility and evidence disputes.

topics.label: Registration certificates, residence cards, applications, fees, and card format

primary_law.note: The dedicated Act and supporting identity-document Act are accepted references. The national Article 12(1) field-10 codes match Regulation 2025/1208 Article 7(2) in Bulgarian, while the 2019/1157 citation, fee linkage, title/implementation evidence, and past transition date remain open dependencies.

implementing_rule.note: The MVR-hosted 19 November 2025 Rules text is link-only, but its official indexed Article 7(1)(10) excerpt routes applications for residence documents under Personal Documents Act Article 59(2)-(4) through the Migration Directorate or regional Migration units. Decree №286/2025, §2, later amended the Rules in SG 109/2025; the amendment's Article 40 changes concern general foreigner-permit routes and do not establish the EU-family card procedure. Current central application/declaration payloads remain link-only. Regulation 2025/1208 requires the 1030/2002 format as implemented by specified Commission decisions; no current card specimen or card-specific issuing instruction was located. The accepted MVR instruction text is consolidated through SG 29/2021; a separate 8-page MVR upload identifying only the 2018 promulgation was not treated as current, and no later amendment is certified.

procedure.note: The MVR service page and directorate directory are reviewed. The indexed Rules excerpt identifies Migration authorities for applications under Personal Documents Act Article 59(2)-(4), but the PDF is not fully retrievable and the later Gazette amendment, current appointment/checklist details, and regional practice remain open. The official IISDA service 870 and 1403 records add bounded filing, processing, collection, and appeal details, but still title the cards under Regulation 2019/1157; they do not establish current card format. Service 1403 also displays both euro and lev amounts, so its fee statement is unresolved.

remedy_or_practice.note: General challenge routes are identified, but no screened card-issuance case or operational evidence is recorded.

open_issues: Reconcile Bulgarian Personal Documents Act transitional § 24(3), whose 3 August 2026 date has passed, with Regulation 2025/1208 Article 8 and its conditional derogation to 3 August 2031; verify current card title, format, implementing decisions and fee treatment from official Bulgarian issuance evidence.

topics.label: Family status, dependency, durable partnership, civil records, and foreign documents

primary_law.note: The EU-citizen Act Additional Provisions § 1(1) defines spouses/cohabiting partners, descendants and dependent ascendants; Article 5 supplies a separate detailed-review route for other dependent/household relatives and serious-health carers. Civil Registration Act Article 70 governs registration of foreign civil-status events for Bulgarian citizens and has treaty/legalisation/translation provisions; it is not itself a general rule recognizing every foreign family relationship for residence. Regulation 2016/1191 simplifies the authenticity/formalities of specified intra-EU documents but does not determine their substantive legal effects. Current substantive treatment of registered partnerships, durable relationships, parenthood and adoption remains open.

implementing_rule.note: Instruction №8121з-1276 Article 20(1) sets foreign-document formalities by treaty/Hague Apostille status; Article 20(2) exempts in-scope Member-State public documents from legalisation under Regulation 2016/1191. That exemption must be applied only to documents and facts within the Regulation; Commission Notice C/2023/1392 offers non-binding guidance on evidence, registration, translation and case-specific authenticity concerns. Current practice for third-country records and unavailable documents is unverified.

procedure.note: The Act and Instruction identify filing and document routes, and Article 5(2) requires a detailed personal-circumstances review for Article 3(2)-type applicants. Regulation 2016/1191 abolishes apostille/legalisation for in-scope Member-State public documents and provides conditional translation simplification; its scope excludes third-country-issued documents and it does not establish a relationship’s substantive legal effect. The current MVR checklist, alternative evidence where a record is unavailable, and specific-authenticity-check criteria remain undocumented.

remedy_or_practice.note: A refusal under Act Article 5(2) must be reasoned and is challengeable under the APC. VAS Decision №11351/2019 recognizes a lawfully concluded same-sex marriage for derivative residence only under the pre-SG 34/2019 Act version. No screened Bulgarian decision addresses civil registration, durable partnership, parenthood/adoption evidence, Regulation 2016/1191 formalities, or third-country document verification.

open_issues: Map substantive eligibility separately for marriage, registered partnership, factual/durable relationships, dependency, parenthood and adoption; distinguish any residence-only recognition from civil registration or wider legal effects.

Reconcile Act Article 5 and Instruction Article 20 with Regulation 2016/1191 Articles 2–8: document categories, certified copies, multilingual standard forms, translation exceptions, apostille/legalisation, and the Regulation’s authenticity-only reach. Keep Civil Registration Act Article 70’s foreign-event registration route separate from evidence supplied in a residence application.

Verify current MVR requirements for third-country records, specific authenticity concerns, unavailable civil records, and alternative proof; review official remedies and case practice. Do not apply blanket checks or extend the Regulation to third-country-issued documents.

topics.label: Retained residence after death, departure, divorce, and permanent residence

primary_law.note: The accepted Act Articles 14–15 cover retained residence after death/departure and relationship termination; Article 16 covers five-year and early worker-derived permanent residence; Article 17 addresses absences; Article 18 concerns the permanent-residence document after over two years away; Article 19 sets the non-EU family-member five-year route and document process. Crosswalked to Directive Articles 12–13 and 16–21 in source-dependencies.json. Legal review remains open on relationship categories and conditions, the child/education route, proof and absence rules, the legal effect of document withdrawal, and how Article 16/19 filing deadlines interact with directly acquired rights.

implementing_rule.note: Instruction №8121з-1276 is the identified document-issuance rule, but its current applicability and detailed evidence requirements for permanent-residence applications under Articles 16 and 19 have not been verified. The accepted text ends at SG 29/2021; no later amendment is certified.

procedure.note: Act Article 16(5) directs specified applicants to file within three days before expiry of extended residence and requires same-day issuance; Article 19(2) sets filing two months before expiry for non-EU family members, paragraph 3 sets issuance within one month, and paragraph 4 provides automatic renewal every ten years. Directive Articles 19–20 instead describe issuance upon application, within six months for a permanent residence card, and application before expiry of the existing card. The exact applicant groups, applicable filing deadlines, evidence route and operational forms need verification.

remedy_or_practice.note: Article 17a requires reasons and an Administrative Procedure Code challenge for refusal of an Article 16 permanent-residence document; no screened VAS or lower-court decision applying Articles 14–19 is recorded. A dedicated refusal/remedy route for Article 19 cases, review effects, and actual Migration Directorate practice remain open.

open_issues: Reconcile Act Articles 14–19 with Directive Articles 12–13 and 16–21, including retained-right conditions for EU and non-EU family members, death/departure/relationship termination, schooling children, early worker routes, absence periods, proof of continuous residence, and whether document withdrawal also affects the underlying right.

Verify Article 16 and Article 19 application timing, required evidence, forms, issuance and challenge routes in current official administrative material; distinguish the right itself from documents that evidence it and compare with Directive Articles 19–21 and 25.
Complete repeatable official VAS and lower administrative-court searches for decisions applying retained and permanent residence provisions; record query scope, result counts and each disposition.

topics.label: Equal treatment, discrimination, and related rights

primary_law.note: The Act and current Commission-hosted anti-discrimination consolidation are accepted; protected grounds and interaction with free-movement claims need issue mapping.

implementing_rule.note: The 2026 State Gazette Rules regulate complaint initiation, form, supporting material, qualified-signature electronic submission, inquiry, hearing, decision, and execution. This is the general Commission route; its application to EU-family residence or visa decisions and relevant protected grounds still needs issue-level review.

procedure.note: Commission complaint guidance and the 2026 Rules identify the general filing route and procedure; jurisdiction, protected-ground fit, access, and linkage to migration decisions remain to be mapped.

remedy_or_practice.note: Commission and Ombudsman routes are identified; no relevant decision or screened case batch is recorded.

open_issues: Check equality remedies, limitation periods, interim relief, and relationship between Commission, Ombudsman, and administrative-court proceedings.
Map the Act and 2026 Commission procedure to EU-family equality claims, including relevant protected grounds, Commission/court overlap, time limits, and screened case practice.

topics.label: Applications, reasons, evidence, deadlines, inaction, and delay

primary_law.note: The MVR-hosted Administrative Procedure Code consolidation through SG 17/2026 (13 February 2026) was crosswalked at Articles 30, 34, 57–60, 84, 149 and 166. APC Article 30 gives a general three-day cure period and restarts the decision clock when defects are cured; Articles 57–59 set general decision periods, deemed-refusal treatment and reasoned-decision content. The dedicated EU-citizen Act contains different service-specific rules: Article 9(4) same-day extended-residence registration and Article 9(5) a seven-day cure; Article 12(4) up to three months for a mobile EU citizen’s non-EU family-member card and Article 12(5) a 14-day cure that pauses that period; Article 16(5) same-day permanent-residence issuance for specified applicants; Article 19(2)–(3) two-month advance application and one-month issuance for a non-EU family member’s permanent-residence card. These special periods must not be replaced by APC defaults. The MVR APC consolidation includes the SG 63/2025 amendments effective 1 July 2026; later amendments after its printed cutoff are not certified.

implementing_rule.note: Instruction №8121з-1276 and Tariff №4 are identified. The accepted Instruction text is consolidated only through SG 29/2021; it gives evidence and filing details but does not establish the complete current procedure. The APC crosswalk distinguishes its general three-day defect-cure rule from the Act’s seven-day Article 9(5) and 14-day Article 12(5) special cure periods. The current fee schedule does not itself establish which fees or exemptions apply to a specific EU-family application; current fee handling and any post-2021 Instruction amendments remain open.

procedure.note: The MVR EU-citizen service page, forms and IISDA services 870/1403 identify filing routes and current published service descriptions. IISDA service 870, checked 25 October 2026, advertises one-month registry timing and optional 3/30-day processing, which does not match the Act’s same-day Article 9(4) issuance for the EU-citizen registration certificate; this is recorded as an unresolved service-description/legal-text discrepancy, not as a change to the statute. Service 1403 provides a separate one-month description for permanent residence. Current regional filing, appointment, completeness-check and actual processing practice are not established.

remedy_or_practice.note: APC Articles 34, 84, 149 and 166 were checked in the MVR consolidation: parties may inspect the file during proceedings, comment on evidence within a period no longer than seven days, and must receive reasons if urgent or important interests displace participation; an express act is generally challengeable within 14 days and silence within two months; the administrative-appeal route provides six months where interested parties were not notified at the start. A challenge generally suspends execution, subject to statutory or separately admitted preliminary execution; a court may suspend preliminary execution on a showing of significant or difficult-to-repair harm. The EU-citizen Act Article 28 separately provides that an appeal against a compulsory measure suspends enforcement except for national-security grounds. Official VAS/administrative-court delay and interim-relief decisions have not yet been screened, and service pages do not establish settled practice. Bounded official EDIS index searches on 25 October 2026 for APC Articles 9, 12 and 28, silence/delay, file access and interim relief found no new on-point published decision; the exact-acronym VAS batch still has 21 matches unreviewed and lower-court searches remain open. Search limitations mean these results do not establish absence.

open_issues: Confirm whether Instruction №8121з-1276 or its evidence/forms provisions were amended after SG 29/2021; reconcile the latest live MVR forms, IISDA service descriptions and the Act’s distinct same-day, three-month, one-month, seven-day and 14-day statutory periods, including the apparent Article 9(4)/service 870 timing discrepancy.

Screen official VAS and administrative-court decisions for incomplete-application notices and cure periods, reasoned refusals, deemed refusal/delay, administrative-file access, and interim relief; record the search date, scope, results and exclusions.

Map APC Article 166 relief against the special EU-citizen Act Article 28 rule and Directive 2004/38 Articles 30–31 for each compulsory measure, including the national-security exception and available urgent remedies.

Verify current regional Migration filing and appointment instructions and the actual service workflow for the 870 and 1403 procedures; the central legal and service links do not establish complete regional operational evidence.

topics.label: Refusal, restriction, expulsion, termination, and removal safeguards

primary_law.note: The accepted EU-citizen Act Articles 22–30 establish exceptional restriction grounds; Article 23 requires personal conduct, degree-of-threat assessment and individual factors, and excludes economic, social-assistance, job-seeking and expired-document grounds. Articles 24–26 address residence withdrawal, expulsion and entry bans; Article 25 includes threat, long-residence/child, non-refoulement and health provisions. Crosswalked to Directive 2004/38 Articles 15 and 27–33 in source-dependencies.json. Legal review remains open on the Article 26 alternative “data” grounds, Article 24(1)(4) health withdrawal, the exact 10-year/child safeguards, and the Act’s scope beside the general Foreigners Act.

implementing_rule.note: The accepted EU-residence Instruction №8121з-1276 addresses residence-document issuance and is consolidated through SG 29/2021; it does not establish detailed implementation of Articles 22–30 restrictions. The Foreigners Act Rules belong to a separate regime; their interaction for EU-family cases and any later restriction-specific instructions remain unverified.

procedure.note: EU-citizen Act Article 27 identifies order-making authorities, requires the order to state appeal period, competent court and voluntary-departure period, sets a one-month minimum subject to a continuing-threat exception, and provides for the order to be explained in an intelligible language by execution authorities. Compare with Directive Article 30 written notice, precise/full grounds (subject to state-security exception), and a one-month period except duly substantiated urgency; current practice and legal reconciliation are open.

remedy_or_practice.note: Articles 28–30 route challenges through the Administrative Procedure Code, suspend enforcement except on national-security grounds, provide for execution after the order is final, and allow revocation requests after three years from finality or earlier after a material change, with a six-month decision period. Directive Articles 31–33 separately address review of facts/law, interim relief before actual removal, exclusion-order lifting after three years from enforcement, and reassessment of delayed expulsion. Whether Bulgarian procedure supplies each safeguard in operation is unverified. Two final VAS decisions are screened: the historical derivative-residence case and a 2026 entry-ban decision requiring individualized evidence; broader expulsion/removal practice remains unreviewed.

open_issues: Obtain a provision-level legal reconciliation of Act Articles 22–30 with Directive 2004/38 Articles 15 and 27–33, focusing on Article 26 grounds, health restrictions, the 10-year and child protections, Article 27 notice/urgency, and Article 28 suspension versus Directive Article 31 interim relief; do not infer incompatibility from wording alone.
Map the EU-citizen Act and Foreigners Act/Rules boundary for non-EU family members, including which authority, grounds and removal procedure apply at each stage.
Review official court decisions and operational evidence on refusal, expulsion, entry bans, interim applications and actual removal; the current screened cases are not a practice survey.

topics.label: Visa processing, refusal reasons, fees, appeal, and judicial review

primary_law.note: The Visa Code applies in Bulgaria under Council Decision (EU) 2024/210 from 31 March 2024. Directive Article 5(2) separately requires free issuance and accelerated handling for qualifying family members; the Handbook supplies non-binding operational guidance. National Ordinance and amendments are accepted references, but the refusal/review provisions have not been fully reconciled.

implementing_rule.note: Current consular tariff, Ordinance and consultation list are identified. Distinguish the Directive no-visa-fee entitlement from listed Visa Code fee categories and possible provider-service charges; exact national scope and consultation exemptions remain open.

procedure.note: Central MFA guidance states a 15-day general processing period with possible extension to 45 days and identifies a route to appeal refusal, but does not explain accelerated processing for qualifying family applicants. Mission procedures and digital-platform implementation remain open.

remedy_or_practice.note: The central MFA page identifies the Ministry and Administrative Court Sofia-city as refusal-review routes. Visa Code Article 32 and Directive safeguards are relevant; exact limitation period, competent forum, suspensive effect, fees, legal aid, and case application are not fully verified.

open_issues: Map Visa Code Article 32 refusal grounds, reasoned notice and appeal language to the MFA’s stated administrative and judicial routes, then verify the applicable Bulgarian filing deadline, forum, fees, suspensive effect and legal-aid route.

Separate visa application fee, optional provider service charges, and no-fee treatment under Directive 2004/38 Article 5(2) and Bulgarian guidance; verify which family categories receive each treatment.

Check accelerated case timing against Directive Article 5(2), the 2024 Visa Code Handbook I and mission-specific appointment availability; do not apply ordinary 15/45-day processing statements without resolving that relationship.

topics.label: Appeal, judicial review, legal aid, and interim protection for residence matters

primary_law.note: Dedicated appeal clauses, general administrative procedure, and the Legal Aid Act are identified; forum/deadline/procedural exceptions need mapping.

implementing_rule.note: The current Legal Aid Act, NBPP organizational Rules, remuneration ordinance, official NBPP and court forms index, and service route are identified. Legal Aid Act Article 22 refers one means-tested category to Social Assistance Rules Articles 9-10; the linked official consolidation ends at SG 44/2023. This does not complete the applicant-rule inventory: current form payloads, live channels, exact means criteria, and application in residence appeals remain open.

procedure.note: Official court-search and directory routes, the Legal Aid Act, NBPP forms, public guidance, service and service-channel pages are identified. The direct page readers did not expose all forms or complete service records; NBPP office-hours and electronic-channel details conflict between Ministry pages. Court motions in pending migration appeals remain distinct from NBPP applications.

remedy_or_practice.note: The accepted current legal-aid and remedy references are supplemented by a final VAS judgment affirming annulment of a five-year EU-citizen entry ban. It is one fact-specific case; interim relief, other residence appeals, current legal-aid means tests and actual legal-aid practice remain unreviewed.

open_issues: Map court competence and time limits; verify the current legal-aid application route and means assessment in residence proceedings; review interim measures and effects of appeal.

Reconcile current Legal Aid Act Article 22 means-assessment routes with the Social Assistance Rules consolidation through SG 44/2023, review current form payloads and channels, and examine legal aid in migration appeal practice.

topics.label: Mission-specific EU-family visa instructions, appointments, checklists, and representation

primary_law.note: The applicable Schengen Visa Code has applied to Bulgaria since 31 March 2024 under Decision 2024/210; Ordinance Article 23(3) gives specified family/household members direct consular access without prior appointment. Mission-specific delegation, provider agreements and legal scope remain to be mapped.

implementing_rule.note: The consular tariff and Ordinance Article 23(3) are identified; local service-fee, direct-lodging, family-fee and exception handling are not verified for the reviewed posts.

procedure.note: Central MFA guidance rechecked 25 October 2026 gives generic timing and appointment text plus broad family exemptions; it does not state the complete accelerated EU-family procedure. Dubai and India links are bounded examples with unresolved contradictions; no mission-wide inference is made.

remedy_or_practice.note: The central refusal routes and one Dubai and two India page sets provide limited practice evidence. Appointment, checklist, timing, territorial scope, representation, provider fee and competent decision-maker issues remain open.

open_issues: Review the MFA mission directory and each relevant post; reconcile Dubai and India appointment instructions with the qualifying EU-family no-prior-appointment provision in Visa Ordinance Article 23(3).
Obtain authoritative checklist and Abu Dhabi scope clarification for the Dubai direct family route; reconcile the two India pages' hours and establish its EU-family procedure.
Map competent decision authority and representation limits for each relevant mission.

Compare the MFA hub’s generic appointment and 15-day instructions with the qualifying-family accelerated route, current Visa Code Handbook guidance and Ordinance Article 23(3); verify how each reviewed mission actually implements direct access.

topics.label: MVR Migration directorate and regional-unit competence, appointment, and filing practice

primary_law.note: National competence and issuing authorities are addressed in the Act and Instruction; territorial implementation is not verified.

implementing_rule.note: National procedure and tariff are identified; local variations are not reviewed. The accepted MVR instruction text is consolidated through SG 29/2021; a separate 8-page MVR upload identifying only the 2018 promulgation was not treated as current, and no later amendment is certified.

procedure.note: The central service route and directorate directory are reviewed. Bounded Pernik, Plovdiv, Burgas, Ruse, Veliko Tarnovo and Stara Zagora pages provide local service evidence; current appointments, complete third-country-family checklists, named decision authorities, exact territorial rules, other directorates, and remedy practice remain open. Sofia is a human-review lead only.

remedy_or_practice.note: Pernik, Ruse, and some other regional pages provide limited filing, schedule or evidence statements; Plovdiv confirms service scope and public counter hours; Burgas lists service 1551 and related forms; Veliko Tarnovo and Stara Zagora confirm local family-service functions. The statements are not generalized across regions, and current appointments, checklists, legal alignment, and regional decisions remain open.

open_issues: Resolve relevant regions and collect official evidence for competence, address, appointment, filing mode, form/checklist, and issuance contact for each unit.
Expand the single Pernik EU-citizen service sample to other regions and third-country family members, and screen regional service or remedy decisions; do not generalize one page.

topics.label: Data handling, access to records, complaints, equality oversight, and ombudsman routes

primary_law.note: The APC, anti-discrimination and Personal Data Protection Acts are identified; MVR Act Article 28 supplies a further request/refusal framework, supplemented by the July 2026 amendment for selected police and unlawful-stay data provisions. Its law-enforcement limits are not assumed to govern routine EU-family residence files.

implementing_rule.note: The MVR-wide 2021 Instruction and 2025 Article 7 amendment set fund-level registers, rules, access profiles, retention review, correction, restriction, deletion and logging. The 50-year fallback applies only absent a different normative act or Minister's order; no Migration-specific fund register, approved rules or retention schedule was located.

procedure.note: The CPDP and Ombudsman routes remain identified. An SDVR-hosted MVR page describes data-rights submission channels and links a one-page form, but the page's law-enforcement framing, Migration-unit routing, and current electronic-delivery channel need verification for EU-family administrative records.

remedy_or_practice.note: MVR rules and a public request route are now identified, alongside CPDP and Ombudsman sources. Their application to Migration administrative records, current filing details, and any relevant published oversight decision remain unverified.

open_issues: Identify the Migration Directorate information fund or funds, their approved Article 27 organisational-technical rules, and any specific retention or periodic-review order before applying the conditional Article 7 default; verify the correct request route, electronic channel, and review/remedy process for EU-family administrative records.

case_law_discovery.finding_2026_10_24: Four targeted official-domain web queries surfaced four items in aggregate. One official legalacts.justice.bg lower-court case lead discusses the boundary between the dedicated EU-family Act and the Foreigners Act for a third-country family member of a Bulgarian national. The full act could not be fetched during follow-up, so it remains unscreened; it is neither accepted as relevant precedent nor excluded. The other surfaced items were a court-hosted Directive text, a judicial-training presentation, and a VAS activity report rather than individual decisions. case_law_discovery.follow_up_2026_10_24: Fifteen additional official-domain web queries identified VAS Decision №11351 of 24 July 2019 in administrative case №11558/2018. mission_tasks_in_review.authority_or_mission: Consulate General of the Republic of Bulgaria in Dubai

current_checklist_or_explicit_no_source_.value: Mission page has no checklist section. external_provider_or_direct_route.value: VFS Global is named for ordinary type-C applicants; the official family-member exception is direct to the Consulate General.

decision_authority.value: MFA states visas are issued by Bulgaria's diplomatic and consular representations; the Dubai Consular Section accepts family-route applications, but the individual decision-maker is not identified.

territorial_competence_and_representatio.value: Dubai contacts state the post serves Dubai and Northern Emirates, omitting Abu Dhabi; a separate MFA UAE-resident visa page describes the direct family route for UAE residents generally. Abu Dhabi applicability unresolved.

open_questions: Does the mission require an appointment for qualifying EU-family applicants despite Ordinance Article 23(3)?
Which checklist applies to the direct family route?
Does the UAE-resident route include Abu Dhabi residents despite the contacts section's stated service area?
